title: SOAP web services
summary: SOAP 1.1 and 1.2 calls, WSDL, faults, WS-Security, large messages and hardening checks. Includes an enterprise test plan (jobs starting ent-).
stack: Any SOAP service (JAX-WS, WCF, Axis, Spring-WS, Zeep, PHP SoapServer)

variables.name: url
variables.guide: The address of the system to test, starting with https:// (or http://) and with no trailing slash, for example https://staging.example.com. Use a system you own, ideally a staging copy. BLASTA runs in a container, so for a service on your own machine use host.docker.internal instead of localhost.

variables.name: soapAction
variables.guide: The SOAPAction of the operation. In the WSDL, <soap:operation soapAction="..."/> under the operation.

variables.name: namespace
variables.guide: The target namespace of the service. Open the WSDL and read `targetNamespace` on the first line.

variables.name: operation
variables.guide: The name of the operation to call. In the WSDL, the names under <portType><operation name=...>.

variables.name: param
variables.guide: The name of one input element of that operation. In the WSDL, find the operation's request message and read the child element's name.

variables.name: value
variables.guide: A value for that parameter, for example an ID that exists.

jobs.name: fetch the WSDL
jobs.notes: Clients fetch the WSDL at start-up, and some on every call (a common performance bug). It is often generated on the fly.

jobs.name: fetch the WSDL (cache bypass)
jobs.notes: Forces regeneration.

jobs.name: SOAP 1.1 call
jobs.notes: A SOAP Fault is returned with HTTP 500, so a Fault counts as an error here. The baseline request: XML parse, dispatch, business logic and response serialisation.

jobs.name: SOAP 1.2 call
jobs.notes: A SOAP Fault is returned with HTTP 500, so a Fault counts as an error here. Same operation with the SOAP 1.2 envelope and content type; some stacks route the versions differently.

jobs.name: WS-Security UsernameToken
jobs.notes: A SOAP Fault is returned with HTTP 500, so a Fault counts as an error here. Adds authentication in the header. Needs SOAP_USER and SOAP_PASSWORD (CLI only; the web UI does not expand environment variables). Token validation is often the slow part.

jobs.name: malformed XML
jobs.notes: Not XML at all. The service must answer with a 400 or a SOAP Fault (HTTP 500) quickly, with no stack trace. Both count as handled.

jobs.name: unknown operation
jobs.notes: A valid envelope calling an operation that does not exist: a Fault is expected.

jobs.name: wrong SOAPAction
jobs.notes: Header does not match the body. Strict services reject it; lenient ones ignore it. Either is fine, but it should not crash.

jobs.name: empty request
jobs.notes: POST with no body.

jobs.name: wrong Content-Type
jobs.notes: XML sent as application/json: expect 415 or 400.

jobs.name: DTD in the request (XXE hardening)
jobs.notes: A harmless inline entity declaration. A hardened parser REFUSES documents with a DOCTYPE (400 or a Fault); a 200 here means DTDs are processed, which is an XML external entity risk.

jobs.name: large message (~100 KB)
jobs.notes: Big requests stress the XML parser (DOM parsers hold the whole tree in memory) and body limits. A 413 or a Fault for too-large input is acceptable.

jobs.name: capacity ramp
jobs.notes: A SOAP Fault is returned with HTTP 500, so a Fault counts as an error here. Ramps the SOAP call to find where latency climbs. XML processing is CPU heavy, so expect a lower ceiling than for JSON.

jobs.name: soak (10 min)
jobs.notes: A SOAP Fault is returned with HTTP 500, so a Fault counts as an error here. Steady load that finds leaks in session state, JAXB/DOM caches and connection pools.

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 01 smoke
jobs.notes: Enterprise plan, step 1 of 10. One request a second for 30 seconds. Run this first, every time: it proves the address, credentials and headers are right and that the environment is up before any real load is applied. Gate: zero errors. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 02 baseline (20% load)
jobs.notes: Step 2 of 10. About a fifth of normal traffic for 5 minutes: the uncontended latency of this request. Every later result is judged against it, so record p50 and p95. Gate: at most 0.5% errors and the default latency targets. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 03 average load (SLO check)
jobs.notes: Step 3 of 10. Normal busy-hour traffic for 10 minutes. The rate is the reference job's rate: raise it to your measured production peak-hour rate. This is the run that proves (or breaks) your SLO. Gate: at most 1% errors, p95 and p99 inside the targets. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

job.name: SOAP web services: 03 average load (SLO check)

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 04 peak load (2x average)
jobs.notes: Step 4 of 10. Twice the average for 10 minutes: the busiest hour of the year plus headroom. Latency may rise, but must stay in SLO; if it does not, you have no headroom. Gate: at most 2% errors, latency targets doubled. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

job.name: SOAP web services: 04 peak load (2x average)

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 05 stress (ramp to 4x)
jobs.notes: Step 5 of 10. Ramps to four times average over 10 minutes, then holds for 2. Finds where it degrades and HOW: gracefully (latency rises, errors stay low) or badly (errors, timeouts, crashes, restarts). Observation only, no gate. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 06 spike (10x in 10 s)
jobs.notes: Step 6 of 10. Reaches ten times average within 10 seconds and holds for 2 minutes: a campaign email, a news link, a failover. Checks autoscaling, queue limits and load shedding. Gate: at most 5% errors, because shedding load is acceptable and crashing is not. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

job.name: SOAP web services: 06 spike (10x in 10 s)

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 07 recovery after the spike
jobs.notes: Step 7 of 10. Run IMMEDIATELY after the spike, at average load for 5 minutes. Latency and errors must return to the baseline from step 2. If they do not, something is stuck: queues, connection pools, GC, an autoscaler cool-down. Gate: same as average load. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

job.name: SOAP web services: 07 recovery after the spike

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 08 soak (1 hour at 60%)
jobs.notes: Step 8 of 10. One hour of steady load. Finds leaks and slow decay in memory, connections, file descriptors, disk, log volume and cache churn. Watch the resource graphs: any line that climbs and never flattens is a finding. Gate: at most 0.5% errors. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

job.name: SOAP web services: 08 soak (1 hour at 60%)

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 09 breakpoint (find the ceiling)
jobs.notes: Step 9 of 10. Ramps to twenty times average over 20 minutes. Stop it when errors pass about 5%: the rate at that moment is your ceiling, and ceiling divided by peak is your capacity margin. Use a production-like environment, never production. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

job.name: SOAP web services: 09 breakpoint (find the ceiling)

jobs.name: SOAP web services: 10 resilience window (failover / deploy)
jobs.notes: Step 10 of 10. Average load for 15 minutes. About 5 minutes in, cause the event you are testing: kill a pod or node, fail over the database, roll out a new version, drain a zone. Errors in the window are your real availability loss. Gate: at most 1% errors overall; read the time series for how long the dip lasted. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

job.name: SOAP web services: 10 resilience window (failover / deploy)

jobs.name: SOAP web services: peak (2x)
jobs.notes: Twice normal for 10 minutes. XML parsing is CPU bound, so SOAP services often saturate a core long before the network. Reference request: SOAP 1.1 call.

jobs.name: SOAP web services: WSDL refetch herd
jobs.notes: Clients refetch the WSDL when they restart, so a rolling restart of 50 client instances is a burst of WSDL requests. Ten times normal for 90 seconds. Reference request: fetch the WSDL.

job.name: SOAP web services: WSDL refetch herd

jobs.name: SOAP web services: authenticated peak
jobs.notes: Three times normal authenticated calls for 10 minutes. Token validation is often the slow part. Reference request: WS-Security UsernameToken.

SOAP_PASSWORD.label: SOAP service password
SOAP_PASSWORD.guide: The password of that service account.

SOAP_USER.label: SOAP service user
SOAP_USER.guide: A service account for WS-Security UsernameToken authentication, from the service's administrator.
